predicates.name: true_diff_established
predicates.question: Is the diff under test the PR's own change against its true merge base?
predicates.procedure:
Resolve merge_base = merge-base(base_branch, head). The unit is
merge_base...head.

If the pin is a squashed commit already on the base branch, the commit IS
the PR and the unit is pin^..pin.

A stacked PR whose parent is unmerged has a merge base below the parent's
work. Establish the parent first; the unit excludes the parent's hunks.
predicates.unresolved_when:
The base branch is ambiguous, the head has been force-pushed past the
recorded pin, or a stacked parent cannot be identified.

predicates.name: ships_to_runtime
predicates.question: Does at least one changed file end up inside a deployed runtime artifact?
predicates.procedure:
Classify each changed path by role. YES if any path is compiled, bundled,
interpreted, baked into an image, or read as input by the running system.

EXCLUDED (do not ship): prose docs (*.md outside a runtime prompt/content
dir, docs/), tests and fixtures (*_test.go, *.test.*, *.spec.*, __tests__/,
testdata/, fixtures/, mocks/), lockfiles, editor/IDE config, and CI
workflow definitions (.github/workflows/).

TWO EXCLUSIONS THAT ARE WRONG AND MUST NOT BE APPLIED:
  * Container/build config DOES ship when it changes the produced artifact's
    contents or entrypoint (base image, installed packages, CMD/ENTRYPOINT,
    build flags). Only build config with no effect on the artifact is
    excluded.
  * Prose that the running system READS is a runtime input, not docs. Agent
    prompts, skill bodies, policy text, and templated content ship even
    though they are markdown.
predicates.unresolved_when:
A changed path's role cannot be determined from the tree (no build config
references it and no import reaches it).

predicates.name: behavior_delta
predicates.question: Does at least one shipping changed hunk alter what the program does at runtime?
predicates.procedure:
For each hunk in a P1-shipping file, compare merge_base to head. YES if the
hunk alters a value computed, stored, returned, rendered, or transmitted,
or alters control flow.

NO for behavior-preserving transformations only: rename, move, extract,
inline, reformat, comment, type-only annotation, and mechanical codegen
output whose inputs did not change.

A dependency bump is NO unless a call site in the diff observes changed
behavior from the new version.

Record the set of hunks that answer YES. Downstream predicates say
"behavior-carrying hunk" and mean exactly this set.
predicates.unresolved_when:
A hunk's runtime effect depends on code not present in the tree (a vendored
binary, a remote service contract, an unpinned generated artifact).

predicates.name: flag_removal_only
predicates.question: Do the behavior-carrying hunks only delete flag evaluations and keep one variation's behavior?
predicates.procedure:
YES if every behavior-carrying hunk removes a flag evaluation and inlines
one of its variations, and no hunk introduces behavior that was in neither
variation at merge_base.
predicates.unresolved_when:
The removed key's variations at merge_base cannot be read, so "kept one
variation" is uncheckable.

predicates.name: removal_changes_customers
predicates.question: Does deleting this flag change what real customers get: does the flag still serve the variation the change deletes to real customers who actually reach the changed code?
predicates.procedure:
Asked only when the change is a flag removal that keeps one
variation's behavior (P3 YES).

YES only if both hold:

1. Still serving the other side. In at least one user-facing
   production environment in the LAUNCHDARKLY STATE section, the
   removed flag still serves the variation whose code the change
   deletes to some real users at the merge date (a fallthrough, a
   rule, a percentage, or individual targets that serve it).
   Internal, staging, test or demo environments don't count.
2. Those users reach the changed code. The feature, page, endpoint or
   job whose behavior the deletion changes is deployed and reachable
   in that environment. A path that environment never runs doesn't
   count: a feature not deployed there, a page or form not offered
   there, or code that another check keeps off there.

NO if either part fails or the evidence doesn't show it: the flag
already serves the kept variation to every real user in every
user-facing production environment, the only users who still get the
deleted variation never reach the changed code, or that they do can't
be shown from the evidence and the repository. Leaning no: a removal that can't be shown to change anything
for real customers is cleanup.
predicates.unresolved_when:
The removed flag's state in a user-facing production environment can't
be read at all.

predicates.name: reader_compat_only
predicates.question: Do the behavior-carrying hunks only teach a reader to accept a format no writer in the tree emits yet?
predicates.procedure:
YES if every behavior-carrying hunk extends a parser/decoder/deserializer
to accept an additional input shape, AND no writer in the tree at
merge_base or head emits that shape, AND no hunk changes the handling of
input already accepted at merge_base.

When the writer is outside the tree and the packet has EXTERNAL REPO
ACTIVITY for it, that is the evidence for the external writer: a PR
there that makes it emit the new shape, RELEASED by the merge date,
means a writer emits it (NO). One merged but NOT released by the merge
date means no deployed writer emits it yet. Cite the diff hunk; name
the external PR number in the evidence.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Whether a writer emits the new format depends on a service outside the
tree, and the packet has no EXTERNAL REPO ACTIVITY showing whether that
writer's change had shipped.

predicates.name: diff_gate_encloses_all
predicates.question: Is every behavior-carrying hunk inside a flag evaluation that the diff itself wires?
predicates.procedure:
For each behavior-carrying hunk, find the nearest enclosing flag
evaluation in the head tree that the diff added or modified. YES only if
EVERY behavior-carrying hunk has one.

Enclosed means that on one side of its gating flags, users get exactly
their merge_base behavior. Either side counts: usually the flag off, but a flag wired backwards -- on
brings back the old behavior, off gives the new -- still switches the
change off. A hunk whose change shows up on both sides of its gating
flags is not enclosed, even if it sits syntactically inside the new
evaluation.

Dominance in control flow is the usual way to show it -- the hunk is
inside the conditional, or after an early return on it. Proximity in
the file is not: a hunk in a sibling branch of the conditional is not
enclosed.

A hunk that runs whatever the flag says is still enclosed when its
change can only be observed through the gated path: a table, column,
or store that only gated code reads or writes; a service or handler
built at startup that only gated code calls; a function only gated
code calls. Show it: cite the gate, and cite every reader or caller of
the change in the packet, each behind the gate. If the packet does not
show every reader or caller, the hunk is not enclosed.

Data gate. A hunk whose code runs whatever
the flag says, but only acts on records -- rows, a column, a stored
field, a record of some kind or status -- that only code behind the
flag writes, counts as behind that flag, like a flag check on the code
path: until the flag is on there is nothing for it to act on. Here it
is the writers, not the readers, that must be behind the gate: cite
the gate over the writes, and show every line that writes those
records, each behind it (a DATA GATES entry in the question lists them,
checked against head; cite its lines of the changed files). Records
that already exist count as written: if ungated code writes them now,
or wrote them before this change, they are there to act on, and the
hunk is not enclosed. If the packet does not show every writer, the
hunk is not enclosed. Whether the flag still withholds the change is
P7/P8's question, from its merge-date state: a flag fully on in the
main production environment protects nothing, and the change is then
judged on its own.

A hunk whose only change is WHICH flags gate existing code -- swapping
one flag for another, or combining flags -- is enclosed by all of the
flags involved, old and new together: its change can only show when at
least one of them is on. Cite every one of those evaluations; whether
they actually withhold the change from users is P7/P8's question,
answered from their merge-date state.

Core enclosure. Enclosure is judged on the change's core behavior: what
the change exists to add or alter -- what the PR is for, and what most of
its behavior-carrying hunks build. YES when one side of the gating flags
withholds that core behavior, even if some hunks outside them run regardless, as
long as each such hunk is incidental to the core: setup or wiring the
gated code needs, a log line or metric, a guard, a refactor, a small
adjustment of existing code made for the gated feature. Cite the gate
over the core, and name each hunk outside it with why it is incidental.

NO when a hunk outside every gate is a change of its own: a separate
fix, feature or behavior change a user would notice apart from the gated
feature, or one that can fail a request, stop startup, or corrupt stored
data. Record which hunks fall outside.
predicates.unresolved_when:
A hunk's enclosure depends on a call through an interface with more than
one implementation in the tree and the dispatch cannot be resolved
statically.

predicates.name: ancestor_gate_encloses_all
predicates.question: Is every behavior-carrying hunk dominated by a flag evaluation that already existed at merge_base?
predicates.procedure:
Same enclosure test as P5, walking up from each hunk through callers,
route guards, and wrapping components, using only evaluations present at
merge_base. YES only if every behavior-carrying hunk is dominated --
judged, as P5 judges it, on the change's core behavior: YES when the
pre-existing gate(s), off, withhold what the change exists to add or
alter, even if some hunks outside them run regardless, as long as each
such hunk is incidental to that core -- setup or wiring the gated code
needs, a log line or metric, a guard, a refactor, a small adjustment of
existing code made for the gated feature. Cite the gate over the core,
and name each hunk outside it with why it is incidental. NO when a hunk
outside every gate is a change of its own: a separate fix, feature or
behavior change a user would notice apart from the gated feature, or
one that can fail a request, stop startup, or corrupt stored data.

Data gate. A hunk that only acts on records that only code behind a
flag writes is dominated by that flag, as P5 says, when the flag existed at merge_base: cite the gate over the
writes and every writer, from a DATA GATES entry in the question or the
changed files. Records that ungated code writes, or wrote before this
change, leave the hunk outside. Writers behind different flags are
alternative ways in: record one `gate_paths` path per writer.

When a YES rests on more than one enclosing flag, say how they
combine, because P8 reads their state by it:
  - `"gates": "all"` -- the change runs only when every cited
    enclosing flag is on: nested gates, such as a product-access check
    around a page and a feature flag around the control inside it.
  - `"gates": "any"` -- any one of them alone reaches the change:
    alternative ways in, such as two pages, each behind its own flag,
    that both open it.
  - a mix -- list the ways in instead, in `"gate_paths"`: one list per
    way in, holding the flags that must all be on for it, e.g.
    `[["access", "flags-page"], ["access", "ai-configs-page"]]` for one
    outer check over two pages that each have their own flag.
Name each flag by its key, as cited. Give neither for a single flag,
or when the evidence does not show how they combine: the flags are
then read as alternative ways in, so any one that exposes the change
exposes it.

When a cited flag is not on/off -- it serves a string, number or JSON
value, and the code takes the changed path only for some of them --
say which value(s) the changed code runs under, as the code compares
them: `"gate_values": {"<key>": ["<value>", ...]}`, citing the line
that compares it. P8 then reads whom the flag serves those values to;
a value that is not one of the flag's variations is served to nobody.
Leave it out when every value reaches the changed code, or when the
evidence does not show which do: the flag is then read as exposing
whenever it is on.

Caller coverage. A changed unit -- a function, method, component,
hook, endpoint or resolver -- that no single gate dominates is still
enclosed when a CALLER COVERAGE entry in the question shows every way
to reach it is behind a flag that existed at merge_base, or leaves the
new behavior off (a caller that passes a value keeping the new branch
from running); a caller in a test or story is not a way in. Only the
entries shown count: each was checked against head, including a
search for every other caller. Cite each caller's gate. When the
callers sit behind different flags, record them as alternative ways in
with `gate_paths`: one path per caller, holding the flags that must
all be on for it. A caller in a client repository (a frontend screen
over a backend resolver or route, written `<repository>:<path>`)
counts when the CALLER COVERAGE entry shows it: it was checked in that
repository at its pinned commit, including a search of that repository
for every other caller, and its flag is read from that repository's
LaunchDarkly project. Outside such an entry, a gate in a different
repository, or on a different tier (a frontend gate over a backend
hunk), does not dominate. Caller coverage does not reach an operation
customers call with their own code (a published API operation, or one
that accepts a user API token): they reach it whatever calls it, in
this repository or a client. A flag checked on that operation's own
request path is not caller coverage but a gate like any other: route
middleware, a guard or loader registered for its route, or a check in
its handler, that refuses or redirects the request unless the flag is
on stops every caller, a customer's own code included.

The ancestor gate is usually NOT in this diff. The packet's search for
it is bounded: the changed files' own merge_base flag evaluations, plus
the REFERENCED FILES (one-hop callers/renderers of a changed file that
sit behind a flag check -- see mechanical.py's
find_referenced_context). A citation into a REFERENCED FILE is
legitimate evidence, on equal footing with a diff citation.

If that bounded evidence shows no pre-existing gate dominating some
behavior-carrying hunk -- including when there are no REFERENCED FILES
at all -- the answer is NO. Do not answer UNRESOLVED because a gate
might exist further away than what is shown: absence within the
bounded search is the definition of NO for this predicate (see
closed_world_note). Never cite or assume a gate from memory or general
familiarity with the codebase.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Same as P5, or the walk leaves the tree (the caller is another
service). NOT "a gate might exist beyond what the packet shows" --
that is NO, per the procedure.

predicates.name: gate_state_resolved
predicates.question: Is the enclosing gate's evaluated state readable for every user-facing production environment as of the merge date?
predicates.procedure:
For the key(s) recorded by P6, read per-environment targeting as of the
merge date: on/off, rules, and the default. Required for every environment
classified user-facing-production.

Derivation is allowed where it is sound: unchanged-since-merge, or
reconstructed from the earliest post-merge audit entry's previousVersion.
A basis must be recorded per environment.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Any user-facing production environment's state at the merge date cannot be
read or soundly derived.

predicates.name: gate_withholds_from_all_users
predicates.question: In every user-facing production environment, does the gate's evaluated state withhold the changed behavior from all real users?
predicates.procedure:
Using the state P7 read, evaluate the gate against the audience of each
user-facing production environment. YES only if, in every such
environment, no real user receives the variation that exposes the
behavior-carrying hunks.

Off for everyone: YES. Targeting only internal/dogfood/staff contexts:
YES. Any percentage rollout above zero to real users, or any rule matching
real users: NO.

More than one gate key. When P6 recorded how its flags combine
(`gates` / `gate_paths`), read them per way in: in an environment, a
way in exposes the change only if every flag on it exposes there, and
the environment exposes the change if any way in does. So for nested
gates (`all`) one flag that still withholds keeps the change withheld.
When P6 recorded nothing, the flags are alternative ways in: any one
that exposes the change exposes it. A flag whose state is unknown
matters only when the known ones do not settle it.
predicates.unresolved_when:
A targeting rule references a context attribute whose population cannot be
determined (an opaque segment with no readable membership).

predicates.name: gate_holds_back_in_main_production
predicates.question: In the main production environment, does the enclosing gate still hold the change back from some real users?
predicates.procedure:
Asked only when an existing gate encloses the change (P6 YES), its
state was read (P7 YES), and it does not withhold the change from
every real user in every user-facing production environment (P8 NO).

Using the state P7 read, for the main production environment only (the
profile's `main_production`): YES when the gate does not serve the
change to every real user there at the merge date -- the flag is off,
serves only internal contexts, serves only a cohort (rules or
individual targets), or serves a partial percentage. NO when it serves
the change to every real user there (`serves: all`). Other user-facing
environments (EU, federal) do not enter: a flag fully on in main
production does not protect the change, even if other regions still
have it off.

Targeting is read as P8 reads it (`serves`, sources.serving). A flag
whose targeting was not read (a multivariate flag, an audit entry that
carried only `on`) counts as serving everyone when it is on: the
reading that errs away from a false already-flagged.

More than one gate key. Read P6's `gates` / `gate_paths` as P8 does
(none recorded: the flags are alternative ways in). The change reaches
every real user in main production only if some way in has every flag
on it serving everyone there: then NO. Otherwise YES. A flag whose
main-production state is unknown matters only when the known ones do
not settle it.
predicates.unresolved_when:
The main production environment's state of a flag that decides it
cannot be read.

predicates.name: candidate_exists_at_base
predicates.question: Does a candidate reuse key exist in flag definitions at merge_base?
predicates.procedure:
Collect candidate keys: keys evaluated in sibling hunks of this diff, keys
evaluated in the enclosing module/route/component, and keys in the repo's
flag definitions whose name matches this feature. A key the feature flag
search verified as releasing the feature this change belongs to (a chain
of lines from its evaluation to the feature's own entry, and from that
entry to the changed code) is a candidate too.

For each, confirm the key EXISTS in flag definitions at merge_base. A key
this diff creates is not a reuse candidate -- there is nothing to reuse.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Flag definitions are not in the tree and the registry cannot be read at
the merge date.

predicates.name: candidate_not_fully_released
predicates.question: Does at least one REUSE CANDIDATE still withhold its own feature from some real users?
predicates.procedure:
Apply the P8 withholding evaluation to EACH candidate P9 found, over its
own feature. YES if at least one candidate is withheld from some real
users in the main production environment. Record which candidates are;
only those are reuse candidates from here on.

A candidate serving its exposing variation to all real users of the
main production environment is not a release lever any more, even
while other regions (EU, federal) still hold it back: production users
already get the change, and gating a change behind it withholds it from
none of them (ruling R5). Neither is an archived flag, whatever its last
served state.
predicates.unresolved_when: P7 unresolvability applies to every candidate.

predicates.name: candidate_evaluates_in_feature
predicates.question: Does all of this change belong to the feature of at least one still-withheld REUSE CANDIDATE?
predicates.procedure:
The candidates are the keys P11 found still withholding (listed in the
question). Check each one.

A candidate's FEATURE is the behavior its evaluation switches: the
branch, component, route or handler that runs only when the candidate
serves its exposing variation, and what that code produces. YES if
EVERY behavior-carrying hunk changes that behavior -- it edits code
inside the candidate's on arm, code reached only from it, or the output
that code produces. A change only partly inside a candidate's feature
is not that feature's change: some of it would ship as part of other
features, so that candidate does not qualify. Name the qualifying
key(s).

Being evaluated in the same file, function, module, route, component or
service as the change does not by itself make the change part of a
candidate's feature, and neither does a candidate evaluated only in a
different feature that this change calls. NO if no candidate qualifies.

A candidate the feature flag search found comes with its lines (FEATURE
FLAG SEARCH in the question): its feature is what its entry -- the
route, page, registration, handler or module the chain ends at --
reaches when it is on. The same test applies: YES only if every
behavior-carrying hunk is inside that feature.
predicates.unresolved_when: P5/P6 dispatch unresolvability applies.

predicates.name: candidate_off_withholds_change
predicates.question: Would the off arm of one of the qualifying REUSE CANDIDATES withhold every behavior-carrying hunk?
predicates.procedure:
The candidates are the keys P10 found this change belongs to (listed in
the question). For each, place the behavior-carrying hunks under that
candidate's off arm and check whether, with it off, users get exactly
their merge_base behavior for every hunk. YES if, for at least one of
those candidates, they do; name that key. A key P10 did not qualify
cannot make this YES.

This is the enclosure test of P5 applied hypothetically, with P5's
definition: withheld means the change does not show, not that the code
does not run. A hunk that still executes with the candidate off but
produces exactly its merge_base behavior is withheld; a hunk whose
change shows up with the candidate off is not. It asks whether the key
CAN cover the change, not whether covering it is worthwhile.
predicates.unresolved_when: P5 dispatch unresolvability applies.

predicates.name: stated_separate_release_plan
predicates.question: Is there a stated fact that this change releases on a different schedule, or to a different audience, than the reuse key's feature?
predicates.procedure:
The reuse key is the one P12 named (given in the question, with the
owners of its evaluation sites). When the walk reaches this question
because the enclosing gate still holds the change back in main
production (P33 YES) and P12 named no key, the reuse key is that
enclosing gate (named in the question). An EVIDENCE test, not an
assessment of separability. YES requires a stated fact of one of
exactly two kinds:

  (a) the PR body or a linked issue names a launch date, audience, or
      rollout plan for THIS change, and that plan differs from the
      reuse key's feature's; or
  (b) CODEOWNERS assigns every changed path to an owning team that does
      not own any of the reuse key's evaluation sites.

Either one alone is sufficient -- they are alternatives, not conjuncts.

Absent both, the answer is NO.
predicates.unresolved_when:
(a) is present but cannot be attributed: the PR names a launch plan
without making clear whether it governs this change or the reuse key's
feature as a whole. Or (b) is ambiguous: CODEOWNERS lists several owning
teams for the changed paths and at least one of them also owns one of
the reuse key's evaluation sites.

predicates.name: new_user_reachable_surface
predicates.question: Does the diff add a surface a non-employee user can reach, or an entry point that changes what customers get?
predicates.procedure:
YES if the diff adds an HTTP route, RPC method, GraphQL field or mutation,
screen, navigable flow, CLI command, webhook, or event consumer, AND
either:
  - the activating input can be minted by a non-employee user; or
  - whoever calls it -- an internal service, an operator, a scheduled
    job -- it writes customer-owned data or changes what customers are
    served: their flags or targeting, billing, access, or the messages
    they receive. Cite the write or the change.
An entry point only employees or internal services call, that only
reads, or only touches the service operator's own bookkeeping or telemetry, is
NO. But an entry point a customer's action can start -- an automated
job, an agent or assistant run, a workflow a customer triggers -- is
customer-facing, not internal, even if it runs in the operator's own
runtime: its activating input is
one a non-employee user mints -- once something a customer starts
reaches it (Not yet reachable, below).

A new control on an existing page -- a button, toggle, menu item,
filter or action -- that lets users do something they couldn't do
before is a new entry point, once
the page renders it where users reach it (Not yet reachable, below). A
control that only offers, in one place, what users could already do
with existing controls (a shortcut, a bulk version of an existing
per-item action), or that brings a surface to parity with the
product's other surfaces, is not: NO. Cite the existing controls that
already did it. That holds only when the new control offers the action
under the same conditions as the existing one: the same checks on who
sees it and on which objects and states it applies to. Cite the
existing control's conditions beside the new one's. A new control that
offers the action where the existing one withholds it -- it skips a
visibility check, an eligibility test or a permission the existing
control applies, shown in the packet -- lets users do something they
couldn't before: YES.

The same holds for an API: a new
kind of input on an existing operation that lets customers do
something they couldn't before -- a new type of entry, a new mode, a
new kind of object they can send -- is a new entry point. An optional
parameter that only adjusts what the operation already did is not.

An entry point added only so something clients already use stops
failing -- a page or link that returned 404 or 500 at merge_base, a
route a shipped client already calls -- repairs an existing surface; it
is NO. Cite what already used it and how it failed. Whether the repair
itself needs a flag is decided later (P21, P23).

"Can be minted by a user" is the operative half. An endpoint reachable
only from an internal network with no user-facing caller is NO; an
endpoint a user's browser can call is YES even with no in-repo caller
-- unless nothing in production reaches it yet (Not yet reachable,
below).

When the PUBLISHED API LOOKUP shows an operation's route binding, that
is the evidence for the minting half. A binding that accepts a user
session or user API token means a non-employee user can mint the input
-- whether or not the operation is in the public spec: publication and
reachability are separate questions. Internal / employee-only auth means
they cannot.

Not yet reachable (backend work that only a
coming, not-yet-visible UI uses needs no flag of its own -- that UI's
flag covers it). An entry point that nothing in production can reach
yet at head is not a surface users can reach yet: NO. That is when no
caller in this change or at head calls it, when its only caller lands
in a separate change, or when it is not registered, mounted or linked
anywhere users or a customer-started run reach -- defined, even
registered, but no caller, route, prompt, job or client that ships
sends it input. This holds for the entry points above too: a new control that nothing renders or links to yet, and an
agent-run, job or workflow path that nothing a customer starts reaches
yet. It does not hold for an operation customers call with their own
code -- a published API operation, or one that accepts a user API
token: customers reach it once it is mounted, whatever calls it in the
repo. Whether a not-yet-reachable entry point needs a flag is decided
when its caller ships; that later change is the one to weigh. Cite
where it is (or isn't) registered, mounted or linked, and that nothing
at head calls it.

Not gateable. A capability defined only by content running code cannot
put behind a flag -- prompt or skill text an agent loads, a Dockerfile or
image configuration, build configuration -- is NO.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Who can mint the activating input depends on gateway or network config not
in the tree.

predicates.name: audience_timing_surface
predicates.question: Does the diff introduce or alter announcement-class content shown to users who did not ask for it?
predicates.procedure:
YES if a behavior-carrying hunk adds or changes a banner, interstitial,
modal, product tour, onboarding step, promotional offer, or push/in-app
notification that appears without the user requesting it -- or an
email, SMS, or other outbound message sent to customers or their users,
or an automated action taken on their behalf, that they did not
request.

REQUESTED means the user, or the organization they belong to, turned on
what produces it: content or an action produced by an automation,
integration, alert, schedule or bot the customer enabled, installed or
configured is requested, and a change to what it produces within that
existing scope is not unprompted. It is unprompted when the change makes
it reach users or accounts that had not turned it on, or makes it produce
a kind of content or action it did not produce before.

Matched on surface class. Technical risk is not part of this test -- who
sees it and when is itself the release decision.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Whether the surface renders unprompted depends on host-application
configuration outside the tree.

predicates.name: public_contract_delta
predicates.question: Does a behavior-carrying hunk change the observable contract of an interface a separate client reads?
predicates.procedure:
YES if a hunk changes a status code, error shape, field presence or type,
pagination, ordering, a limit, or a default -- the value the interface
uses or creates when the caller leaves it unset -- on an EXISTING interface that either
  - is published in customer-facing API documentation or in a versioned
    public schema at merge_base; or
  - is consumed by a separate client -- a frontend, SDK, CLI, or another
    service -- shown in the packet reading what changed (the status it
    branches on, the field it reads). Cite that reader.
A request the change makes differently (what it sends) is not a change
to the contract the interface returns. An interface the diff adds has
no contract yet; whether it needs gating is P15's question.

A response that failed at merge_base -- an error, a crash, a request
the server could not complete -- and now succeeds is a repair, not a
contract change: no client could have been relying on the failure.
Except a guard: when the change removes or loosens a check that
refuses an action on purpose -- an approval requirement, a permission
or role check, a plan, entitlement or policy limit -- so requests it
was meant to refuse at merge_base now go through, that IS a contract
change. Cite the guard line at merge_base. A guard that refused
requests it was meant to allow (the PR or a test the diff adds shows
the refusal was the bug) is repaired, not removed. A validation error,
a lookup that wrongly found nothing, or a crash is not a guard: those
stay repairs.
A request that fails at merge_base and still fails at head, where only
how the failure is reported changes -- a server error (5xx) that now
returns a client error (4xx), or a clearer error message or body -- is
a repair too, not a contract change: no client could have been relying
on the failure succeeding. It stays a contract change when the failure
moves the other way (a client error that now returns a server error),
or when a separate reader at merge_base branches on the old status or
error code (cite that reader line at merge_base). This exception is
only for requests that fail both before and after: a request that
succeeds at merge_base and now fails IS a contract change, and so is
any change to what a successful response returns.

NOT a contract change:
  - rejecting input the interface's own documentation, schema or
    validation at merge_base already treats as invalid, or malformed
    input the operation cannot parse or carry out (a regular
    expression, query or expression that does not compile), even with
    a new status code or error body;
  - fixing a wrong answer: a response that contradicted the
    interface's own documented responses, or returned incorrect data
    (a wrong count, total or value), now matching them;
  - removing a field, parameter, path or shim nothing reads: no
    reader in the packet, and none in the published docs.
STILL a contract change: a successful response that behaved as
documented now changes to follow an outside standard (an HTTP status
meaning, an OAuth spec, an RFC); and any new or changed successful
response. A request that fails before and after and only reports its
failure better (above) is not one, even when its new status follows
an HTTP status meaning.

Cite the documentation, schema or validation an exception rests on:
for a published operation, the documented responses the PUBLISHED
API LOOKUP lists for it at merge_base (for incorrect data, the code or
test that shows the old answer was wrong; for malformed input, the
code that fails to parse or run it). Without it the exceptions
don't apply. That is not a reason for UNRESOLVED: when the packet
shows no documentation that the old response was wrong, answer by
the rest of this procedure.

Publication must be established from the tree or the published docs -- not
from the route looking public.

When the packet has a PUBLISHED API LOOKUP section, it is that
evidence, read from the repo's published spec at merge_base: an
operation marked PUBLISHED is published, one marked NOT PUBLISHED is
not. Cite the hunk that changes the contract; the lookup establishes
publication. A hunk the lookup matched to no operation is not shown to
be on a published interface -- use other evidence in the packet if
there is any.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Publication evidence conflicts with in-code annotations -- e.g. the route
carries `@Hidden` or an internal-only tag while appearing in customer
documentation. Do not resolve this by preferring one source. Escalate.

Or a hunk changes the contract's shape -- a status code, error shape,
field presence or type, pagination, ordering, or a limit -- on an existing
interface, and the packet establishes neither publication nor a separate
reader. Whether a client relies on it cannot be decided from the packet:
the reader is often in another repository. Neither NO (the client may
exist) nor YES (none is shown) follows from the evidence.

predicates.name: interaction_change
predicates.question: Does the diff change an interaction that a user experiences on an existing screen without opting in?
predicates.procedure:
YES if, on a path a user reaches without configuring anything, a hunk
changes an INTERACTION on an existing screen that users must now
perform differently to finish a task they already do: a control they
use moves to a different page or menu, or is replaced by a different
kind of control that works differently, or is removed with its action
no longer available elsewhere; or a step is added to or removed from a
flow.

NOT an interaction change: a
changed DEFAULT CHOICE -- a control's initial setting, an initial
toggle or filter state, a default sort, ordering or page size, which
view or tab opens first -- when every choice is still there for the
user to pick. A changed default in a published API is a contract
change, P19's question, not this one's.

NOT an interaction change: a
control moved within the same page; a control swapped for a newer
component that people use the same way; removing a non-essential extra
(a promo tip, a feedback or survey button, a help link) when nothing
people need for their work goes away.

NOT an interaction: changing a screen's content, copy, or
presentation (what text or styling a control has, how a value is
rendered), or when and how its data is fetched. Those change what the
user sees, not a choice they make or a way they act; whether they need
a flag is decided later (P21, P22).

A path only employees or the service operator's own staff use -- an
internal tool, an admin console, a developer utility -- is not a path
a user reaches: NO. The users this protects are customers. A path a
customer's action can start -- an automated job, an agent or
assistant run, a workflow a customer triggers -- is customer-facing,
not internal, even if it runs in the operator's own runtime.

Line count is not part of this test.

A new capability the diff adds is not an interaction users already
had -- whether it needs gating is P15's question, not this one's.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Whether the changed interaction is reachable without user
configuration depends on stored per-user settings whose distribution
cannot be read.

predicates.name: shared_path_load
predicates.question: Does a behavior-carrying hunk add new work to a production path that every customer's traffic runs through, where that work failing or slowing down would affect that traffic?
predicates.procedure:
YES if a behavior-carrying hunk adds, on such a path, work that runs for
each request, record, event, job run, or session -- a call to another
service or data store, a write, a per-item metric, log, or trace record,
or a check that can block or reject the operation -- AND that work can
fail, slow down, or multiply load for all traffic on the path. Cite the
hunk and the path's entry: the ingest handler, route, worker loop, or
startup code it runs in.

Name that entry by following the calls from it to the changed code, and
name every condition on the way that decides whether the changed code
runs: an argument that is empty or set, a mode or option, a caller's
choice between two functions. The new work itself is never one of those
conditions: a check, lookup or call the change adds runs for every
request that reaches it, whatever it then decides, and a lookup whose
failure fails the request can fail requests it would have let through.
A YES is about the traffic that reaches the new work past those
conditions. When customers'
traffic takes the other side of one (their callers always pass the
value, so only a call without it reaches the change), the path is the
one that side serves, and it is judged as that path: an internal
endpoint, tests, or a small set of accounts is a NO below. A condition
that only turns the work on for a deployment (an environment variable, a
configured target) does not narrow the traffic: judge the path as it
runs once that is set.

NOT new work for this question:
  - the extra read a fix needs to return the right answer: a fix to a
    wrong answer (a count, total or value that contradicted the
    interface's documentation or was incorrect) that now takes
    another query of the same data store to compute it;
  - a metric, log line or trace record that only the team reads -- no
    customer sees it in a chart or acts on it through an alert --
    however many series or records it makes;
  - a check that only rejects input that can't be valid: input the
    interface's own documentation, schema or validation at merge_base
    already treats as invalid, or malformed or oversized input.
Calls, writes, and checks that can reject a valid operation still are.

A path every customer's traffic runs through: data ingestion, a public
or customer-facing API route, a queue worker or scheduled job that
processes all accounts, flag evaluation or delivery, session or process
startup. A route the product's own UI calls on customers' behalf is
customer-facing whether or not it appears in the published API spec:
"internal" means only employees or the operator's own services call it.
A path a customer's action can start -- an automated job, an agent or
assistant run, a workflow a customer triggers -- is customer-facing,
not internal, even if it runs in the operator's own runtime.

NO when the work runs only for a new, opt-in, or already-gated path;
only for internal or employee tools, admin paths, or a small set of
accounts; or only once (a migration, a one-off job). NO when it only
changes existing work -- a different query for the same call, a changed
log message -- without adding a call, a write, or a check.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Whether the path carries all customers' traffic depends on routing or
deployment not shown in the packet.

predicates.name: shared_path_load_contained
predicates.question: Is the new work that made P27 fire unable to degrade the path it runs on, or not something a runtime flag would usefully turn off?
predicates.procedure:
Asked only after P27 answers YES; that finding is given with the
question.

YES only if EVERY piece of new work P27 cites is one of these, each
shown with evidence:
  - Contained: it is sampled or rate-limited (runs for a bounded
    fraction or number of items, not each one); or it runs
    asynchronously, off the operation's critical path, and its failure
    cannot fail the operation; or it is bounded -- a fixed cap on
    items, size, or retries cited in code, or a cardinality the code
    bounds by construction (one series or key per route, handler, or
    operation name -- not per user, record, request, or ID); or it
    fails open under a timeout, the path continuing with its
    merge_base behavior.
  - Not gateable at runtime: it takes effect when deployed or applied
    (a schema or DDL migration, build or infrastructure
    configuration), not when code runs.
  - Not yet live: nothing in production calls it at head.
  - Repair: it only runs for inputs that fail or are mishandled at
    merge_base, so turning it off would only restore that failure.
  - Instrumentation only: a
    metric, log line or trace record that only the team reads -- no
    customer sees it in a chart or acts on it through an alert --
    however many series or records it makes.

NO if any cited work runs for every item with no bound, can block or
fail the operation, or (instrumentation aside) grows along an
unbounded dimension -- per-item rows or writes.
predicates.unresolved_when:
The bound, the asynchronous handoff, or the timeout lives in
configuration or a library the packet does not show.

predicates.name: live_path_risk
predicates.question: Does the change rework a path customers already use in a way that can fail them, shown line by line from a changed line to the customer entry point?
predicates.procedure:
Answered from the risk search, never asked. YES when at least one
finding verified: a changed line the diff adds or modifies in shipping
code, an entry point customers reach (a route or page, a handler bound
to a user session or API token, a job or webhook that runs for
customers) outside tests, and every link between them quoted exactly
at head. The kinds: a new call or write to another service or store, an
existing call or write retargeted, a cache in front of an existing read,
a condition that fails closed when such a call fails, a new customer
action, a removed capability, a stored-data change. NO when nothing
verified, including when the search found nothing. Internal tools,
instrumentation only, code nothing calls yet and repairs of inputs that
already failed are excluded by the search itself.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Never: an unverified finding is not a finding, and NO keeps the verdict
the rest of the tree reached.

predicates.name: signal_counter_signal
predicates.question: Is the change that made this signal fire one a flag would not usefully turn off -- a repair, hardening, presentation only, not yet live, operational records only, a redundant affordance, or not gateable -- with nothing else about it arguing for a flag?
predicates.procedure:
Asked only after P18 or P20 answers YES; that finding is
given with the question. It does not undo the signal: a YES only
means P21 decides between suggested and not-suited, and it can never,
by itself, make a change not-suited.

YES only if BOTH hold:

(a) Every hunk the signal rests on is one of these, each shown with
    evidence:
  - Repair: it only changes the outcome for inputs that fail, error,
    or are mishandled at merge_base, so turning it off would only
    restore that failure. Show the failure: in the code, by a test
    the diff adds that exercises it, or by EXTERNAL REPO ACTIVITY.
  - Hardening: it only removes an unsafe merge_base behavior.
  - Presentation only: it only changes how existing content is
    presented (styling, layout, markup, static copy, accessibility).
  - Not yet live: what it adds has no producer or reader in
    production at head -- a parallel store nothing reads, a table
    only a later change will switch to, a field no caller sends.
  - Operational records only: it only changes the service's own
    telemetry or bookkeeping.
  - Redundant affordance: it only removes a control whose action
    stays available another way. Cite where the action remains.
  - Not gateable: a runtime flag cannot gate it, because it takes
    effect when it is deployed or applied rather than when code runs
    (a schema or DDL migration, build or infrastructure
    configuration), or because the code runs with no flag context.
    Cite what applies it. Code the same diff adds that reads or
    writes the result is a separate hunk and is judged on its own.

(b) Nothing else about it argues for a flag: it adds no entry point or
    user flow, changes no contract clients or other services read, and
    changes no interaction users rely on.

When the packet does not establish (a) for every hunk the signal rests
on, or any part of (b) fails, the answer is NO.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Never. Missing evidence is NO: the suggestion stays firm, the
conservative direction.

predicates.name: user_perceptible_delta
predicates.question: With every cited gate in its merge-date state, does a behavior-carrying hunk change what a real user perceives?
predicates.procedure:
YES if a real user on a path reachable at the merge-date gate state
perceives a difference: rendered output, response payload, an error they
receive, a latency class change, a notification, or persisted data they
can later read.

Employee-only and internal-tool surfaces are NO. Background work with no
user-perceptible consequence is NO. Work a customer's action can start
-- an automated job, an agent or assistant run, a workflow a customer
triggers -- is customer-facing, not an internal tool, even if it runs
in the operator's own runtime:
judge what that customer perceives of it.
predicates.unresolved_when: Reachability depends on gate state that P7 could not resolve.
predicates.role:
The last node before escalation, and it only ever routes to `not-suited`
on NO. It is a veto on a silent skip, not a route to one: a YES here with
no battery signal is precisely the residue 0.4.0 tells a reader to "judge
on the merits", and judging on the merits is what this graph replaces with
an escalation.

predicates.name: presentation_only
predicates.question: Is every behavior-carrying hunk only a change to how existing content is presented?
predicates.procedure:
YES if every behavior-carrying hunk changes only presentation: visual
styling or layout, markup structure, static copy text (including
moving copy into a message catalog, and a display fallback for a
missing value), icons, or accessibility attributes (labels, roles,
aria-*).

NO if any behavior-carrying hunk changes:
  - what data is fetched, sent, stored, or computed, beyond formatting
    it for display;
  - event handling or control flow: what happens on a click, key
    press, submit, navigation, or focus change;
  - which actions, controls, or pages are available. Adding or
    removing a button, link, menu item, or other affordance is not
    presentation-only.

This is a not-suited exit, so a YES needs positive evidence for every
behavior-carrying hunk. When the packet does not establish it, the
answer is NO, not UNRESOLVED.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Never. Missing evidence is NO: the walk continues to escalation, which
is the conservative direction.

predicates.name: failure_path_only
predicates.question: Does every behavior-carrying hunk change behavior only for requests or inputs that fail or are mishandled at merge_base?
predicates.procedure:
YES if, for every behavior-carrying hunk, the only inputs whose outcome
changes are ones that at merge_base end in an error, an exception, a
rejected request, a crash, or silently dropped or incorrect data -- and
every input that is handled correctly at merge_base gets exactly the
same result at head. For each hunk, cite what failed at merge_base.

The failure may be shown by the code itself, or by either of these in
the packet -- cite which:
  - a test the diff adds or changes that exercises the failing input
    and asserts an outcome the merge_base code does not produce (cite
    the test and the merge_base line that fails it);
  - EXTERNAL REPO ACTIVITY showing a client released by the merge date
    already sends that input (name the external PR), so merge_base was
    already receiving it and mishandling it.

A request to an HTTP, RPC, or GraphQL endpoint that fails at
merge_base and still fails at head, now reported as a client error
(4xx) instead of a server error (5xx) or with a clearer error message
or body, counts as failing at merge_base: YES for that hunk. NO if the
failure moves the other way (a client error that now returns a server
error), or if a separate reader at merge_base branches on the old
status or error code: other services and client apps may depend on how
a failure is reported. This is about what an endpoint sends over the
network, not about which error value one function in the same program
hands another.

NO if any hunk changes the outcome for an input handled correctly at
merge_base.

This is a not-suited exit, so a YES needs positive evidence for every
behavior-carrying hunk. When the packet does not establish it, the
answer is NO, not UNRESOLVED.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Never. Missing evidence is NO: the walk continues to escalation, which
is the conservative direction.

predicates.name: perceptible_counter_signal
predicates.question: Is this perceptible change one a flag would not usefully turn off, with nothing about it that argues for a flag?
predicates.procedure:
P21's finding (what a user perceives) is given with the question.

YES only if BOTH hold:

(a) The change is one of these, shown with evidence:
  - Repair: it fixes behavior that is wrong at merge_base, so turning
    it off would restore the bug. Show it by a test the diff adds that
    asserts the corrected behavior, or by the PR's stated bug where the
    code confirms it. PR text alone is never enough.
  - Hardening: it only removes an unsafe merge_base behavior.
  - Not yet live: the capability it adds has no producer in production
    at head.
  - Operational records only: it only changes the service's own
    telemetry or bookkeeping.
  - Redundant affordance: it only removes a control whose action stays
    available another way. Cite where the action remains.
  - Not gateable: a runtime flag cannot gate it (it takes effect at
    deploy time, or the code has no flag context).

(b) Nothing about it argues for a flag: it adds no entry point or user
    flow, changes no contract that clients or other services depend on
    (a status code, error body, field, or ordering they read), and
    changes no interaction users rely on beyond restoring what was
    intended.

When the packet does not establish (a), or any part of (b) fails, the
answer is NO and the change stays escalated.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Never. Missing evidence is NO: the change stays escalated to a human,
the conservative direction.

predicates.name: small_reversible_blast_radius
predicates.question: If this change shipped with a mistake, would the harm stay small and be quickly undone without a flag: few users reached, the failure plain to see, and a revert putting everything back?
predicates.procedure:
Asked only after P18 or P20 answers YES, where the walk would
otherwise suggest a flag; that finding is given with the question.

YES only if all four hold, each from the evidence:

1. Reach. What the change alters isn't on a path where a mistake
   costs much:
     - not authentication, sign-up, sessions or permissions;
     - not billing, pricing, plans or entitlements;
     - not how flags are evaluated, targeted, served or released;
     - not a write, delete or migration of customer data;
     - not results customers act on as fact (metrics, experiment
       results, audit records);
     - not an interface another client or service reads (P19);
     - not work on a path all customer traffic runs through (P27).
2. Failure is visible and bounded. A bad version would show up as
   something users can see and work around: wrong text or layout, a
   control in the wrong place, an action that fails and can be
   retried. It doesn't silently serve or store wrong data, lose what a
   user entered, block a workflow with no other route, or take a page
   or service down.
3. A revert undoes it. Rolling back the deploy restores the old
   behavior for everyone: nothing is written in a new format, no data
   is migrated, and no outside effect (email, webhook, third-party
   call) has already happened.
4. Nothing calls for a controlled rollout. No rollout plan,
   experiment, metric to watch, beta or early-access audience, or
   customer commitment is stated in the PR or the code.

Size is never a reason. A one-line change to sign-up fails (1); a
large rework of a settings page's layout can pass. Answer from what
the change touches and how it would fail, not from how big it is.

NO if any part fails, or the evidence doesn't show it.
predicates.unresolved_when:
Whether the change touches one of the paths in (1), or writes data,
depends on code the evidence doesn't show.
